Pickett's Charge and the high water mark for the Confederacy

Charging the center was the 2nd best plan - Gen Longstreet did not feel that attacking the Federal right at Little Round Top for a second day would be the right move, and only agreed to the attack in the center if only one of his 3 divisions took part. Therefore, Pender's deiviosn was moved to the center between Pettigrew and Anderson. The Hood and McLaws divisions were left out of the fighting, even though Lee relied on Hoods's Texans as his "shock troops" throughout he 1862-63 campaigns. Anderson's inability to follow up Pickett's Charge with reinforcements to hold the line, stemmed, in large part, from havign parts of 2 corps make as imultaneous attack. When Pickett and Pettigre crossed into the Federal lines, this created what we call today a "beachhead", and if Anderson's division had poured into that breach, the day could still have been won.

The number of mistakes that occurred at Gettsyburg, in my mind, can be attributed directly to the death of Gen Jackson at Chancellorsville. The army was split from 2 corps into 3. Weakening Longstreet's Corps by 33%. "Old Pete" was one of the most tenacious generals once the fighting started, but he was by nature, conservative and a protector of his men. If Longstreet had his normal sized Corps, I believe he would have acted much differently at Gettysburg, and would have coordinated the attack on the federal lines, either at Little Round Top or Cemetery Ridge much better than coordinating between 2 different corp commanders, which brings us to point 2 - coordinating an all out assult using two separate commanders is difficult at best, impossible at worst. Lee's inability to step up and take full command at Gettysburg, and allow his generals to dictate both strategy and tactics led to this conundrum. Finally, if Pickett had arrived on time the day prior, and not marched until the morning, the attacks by Ewell's Corps on Culp's and Cemetery Hill , scheduled for 10AM, could have been followed immediately by the coordionated attacks on 2 of Pettigrews divisions, and 1 of Longstreet's, placing the federals in a position of being trapped in the fishhook, and may have necessitated a withdrawal from the ridge to avoid losing their guns.

Overall: Tthe lack of use of Hood and McLaws division, and of Rodes division on July 3rd was a mistake. Having the main assault operated by two corps commanders instead of one was a mistake. Not having Pickett in place when Ewell counterattacked at 10AM was a mistake. The gains of Ewell were lost due to inaction on the other fronts.
Lee not directing the battle as the day progressed, but allowing his 3 generals to direct 3 separate battles left the Rebels without leadership when they needed it the most - following up success with a breakthrough set of fresh troops to take advantage.

Considering that the whole reason for the invasion of Pennsylvania was to gather provisions that the South was unable to provide for men and horses alike, the retreat from Gettysburg was the end of the war. No matter how much Lee might anticipate the movements of the opposing general, without food and clothing for his men, and fodder for his horses, he would never be able to field an army that could actually defeat the federals after that day.
